claim: Brain rhythms have been proposed to facilitate brain function, with an especially important role attributed to the phase of low-frequency rhythms.
source: Brain rhythms have been proposed to facilitate brain function, with an especially important role attributed to the phase of low-frequency rhythms.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field supported by the context of the manuscript and implied citations in the broader literature.

claim: Current methods for real-time phase estimation rely on bandpass filtering.
source: Current methods for real-time phase estimation rely on bandpass filtering, which assumes narrowband signals and couples the signal and noise in the phase estimate, adding noise to the phase and impairing detections of relationships between phase and behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by the description of existing methods and their limitations in the manuscript.

claim: Bandpass filtering assumes narrowband signals and couples the signal and noise in the phase estimate.
source: Current methods for real-time phase estimation rely on bandpass filtering, which assumes narrowband signals and couples the signal and noise in the phase estimate, adding noise to the phase and impairing detections of relationships between phase and behavior.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of bandpass filtering methods.

claim: The state space phase estimator avoids the requirement of bandpass filtering.
source: By tracking the analytic signal as a latent state, this framework avoids the requirement of bandpass filtering, separately models the signal and the noise, accounts for rhythmic confounds, and provides credible intervals for the phase estimate.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the proposed method's capabilities.

claim: The state space phase estimator separately models the signal and the noise.
source: By tracking the analytic signal as a latent state, this framework avoids the requirement of bandpass filtering, separately models the signal and the noise, accounts for rhythmic confounds, and provides credible intervals for the phase estimate.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the proposed method's capabilities.

claim: The state space phase estimator accounts for rhythmic confounds.
source: By tracking the analytic signal as a latent state, this framework avoids the requirement of bandpass filtering, separately models the signal and the noise, accounts for rhythmic confounds, and provides credible intervals for the phase estimate.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the proposed method's capabilities.

claim: The state space phase estimator provides credible intervals for the phase estimate.
source: By tracking the analytic signal as a latent state, this framework avoids the requirement of bandpass filtering, separately models the signal and the noise, accounts for rhythmic confounds, and provides credible intervals for the phase estimate.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the proposed method's capabilities.

claim: The state space phase estimator outperforms current state-of-the-art real-time methods in the contexts of broadband rhythms, phase resets, and co-occurring rhythms.
source: We demonstrate in simulations that the state space phase estimator outperforms current state-of-the-art real-time methods in the contexts of common confounds such as broadband rhythms, phase resets, and co-occurring rhythms.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The method is available as a ready-to-use plug-in for the Open Ephys acquisition system.
source: The method is available as a ready-to-use plug-in for the Open Ephys acquisition system, making it widely available for use in experiments.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the availability of the method.

claim: Many studies have described a relationship between rhythms and behavior.
source: Many studies have described a relationship between rhythms and behavior (Buzsáki, 2006; Haegens and Zion Golumbic, 2018; VanRullen, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Phase has been proposed to coordinate neural spiking locally and potentially, through coherent networks, even globally.
source: Phase has been proposed to coordinate neural spiking locally and potentially, through coherent networks, even globally (Fries, 2015; Maris et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The phase of slow rhythms (3–15 Hz) has shown relationships to dynamics in perception.
source: For example, the phase of slow rhythms (3–15 Hz) has shown relationships to dynamics in perception (Busch et al., 2009; Gaillard et al., 2020; Gregoriou et al., 2009; Helfrich et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Phase-amplitude synchrony is common.
source: Phase-amplitude synchrony is common (Canolty and Knight, 2010; Hyafil et al., 2015), and has been suggested to change in neurodegenerative disease (Hemptinne et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Phase-amplitude synchrony has been suggested to change in neurodegenerative disease.
source: Phase-amplitude synchrony is common (Canolty and Knight, 2010; Hyafil et al., 2015), and has been suggested to change in neurodegenerative disease (Hemptinne et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cross-regional, low-frequency phase synchrony is consistently observed as a correlate of top-down executive control.
source: Cross-regional, low-frequency phase synchrony is consistently observed as a correlate of top-down executive control (Widge et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Most work examining the importance of phase for neural dynamics and behavior has been correlative in nature.
source: Most work examining the importance of phase for neural dynamics and behavior has been correlative in nature.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of the field.

claim: Several methods exist to estimate phase in real-time.
source: Several methods exist to estimate phase in real-time (Blackwood et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2013; Mansouri et al., 2017; Rodriguez Rivero and Ditterich, 2021; Rutishauser et al., 2013; Siegle and Wilson, 2014; Zrenner et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Existing real-time phase estimation methods rely on bandpass filtering, a mechanism to forward predict data (using autoregressive [AR] models or linear extrapolation of phase) and the Hilbert transform to estimate the phase.
source: At their core, these methods rely on bandpass filtering, a mechanism to forward predict data (using autoregressive [AR] models or linear extrapolation of phase) and the Hilbert transform to estimate the phase.
evidence: This is a description of existing methods based on the literature.

claim: Brain rhythms are often non-sinusoidal and broadband.
source: Brain rhythms are often non-sinusoidal (Cole and Voytek, 2017) and broadband (Buzsaki, 2004; Roopun et al., 2008), making development of an accurate bandpass filter difficult.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: By depending on bandpass filters, existing real-time phase estimators are susceptible to non-sinusoidal distortions of the waveform.
source: (1) By depending on bandpass filters, existing real-time phase estimators are susceptible to non-sinusoidal distortions of the waveform, and inappropriate filter choices may miss the center frequency or total bandwidth of the rhythm.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of existing methods based on their reliance on bandpass filtering.

claim: Phase resets cannot be tracked using filters, which control the maximum possible instantaneous frequency.
source: (2) Phase resets, moments when the phase slips because of stimulus presentation or spontaneous dynamics, cannot be tracked using filters, which control the maximum possible instantaneous frequency.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of filter-based methods.

claim: By filtering the observed data directly, existing approaches do not model signal and noise processes separately.
source: (3) By filtering the observed data directly, these approaches do not model signal and noise processes separately. Phase estimates thus represent signal and noise phase together.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of existing methods.

claim: Many existing approaches depend on buffered processing, meaning that current phase estimates are delayed in ways that may not support real-time intervention.
source: (4) Many existing approaches depend on buffered processing (e.g., Fourier or related transforms), meaning that current phase estimates are delayed in ways that may not support real-time intervention.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of existing methods.

claim: Contemporary approaches do not define a measure of confidence in the phase estimate.
source: (5) Contemporary approaches do not define a measure of confidence in the phase estimate.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of existing methods.

claim: Real-time phase simulations using current techniques have produced interesting results.
source: Despite these limitations, real-time phase simulations using current techniques have produced interesting results (Cagnan et al., 2017; Desideri et al., 2019; Hyman et al., 2003; Kundu et al., 2014; Schaworonkow et al., 2018; Siegle and Wilson, 2014; Zrenner et al., 2018), motivating the value of generating better methods to estimate phase causally.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The SSPE method focuses on tracking the analytic signal as a latent process in the observed time series using a model proposed by Matsuda and Komaki, 2017.
source: Rather than filtering the data to identify the rhythm of interest, we focus on tracking the analytic signal (a complex valued entity, representing the amplitude and phase of a rhythm Kramer and Eden, 2016) as a latent process in the observed time series using a model proposed by Matsuda and Komaki, 2017.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the method and its basis in prior work.

claim: The SSPE modeling approach allows a separate estimate of observation noise.
source: This modeling approach allows: (1) a separate estimate of observation noise, (2) a procedure to model and reduce the confounding activity of other rhythms, and (3) a principled method for assessing uncertainty in the real-time phase estimates.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the capabilities of the SSPE method.

claim: The SSPE modeling approach allows a procedure to model and reduce the confounding activity of other rhythms.
source: This modeling approach allows: (1) a separate estimate of observation noise, (2) a procedure to model and reduce the confounding activity of other rhythms, and (3) a principled method for assessing uncertainty in the real-time phase estimates.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the capabilities of the SSPE method.

claim: The SSPE modeling approach allows a principled method for assessing uncertainty in the real-time phase estimates.
source: This modeling approach allows: (1) a separate estimate of observation noise, (2) a procedure to model and reduce the confounding activity of other rhythms, and (3) a principled method for assessing uncertainty in the real-time phase estimates.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the capabilities of the SSPE method.

claim: After first fitting parameters of the state space harmonic oscillator model acausally, the method then tracks the phase in real-time assuming spectral stationarity.
source: After first fitting parameters of the state space harmonic oscillator model acausally, the method then tracks the phase in real-time assuming spectral stationarity.
evidence: This is a direct statement about how the SSPE method operates.

claim: The comparison is limited to the real-time methods proposed in Zrenner et al., 2020, and Blackwood et al., 2018.
source: We limit our comparison to the real-time methods proposed in Zrenner et al., 2020, and Blackwood et al., 2018, methods which provide an estimate of phase on receipt of each new sample of data and have readily available reference code.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the scope of the comparison.

claim: A standard method for non-real-time phase estimation is an acausal finite impulse response (FIR) filter followed by a Hilbert transform.
source: We additionally apply a standard method for non-real-time phase estimation (an acausal finite impulse response [FIR] filter followed by a Hilbert transform; Lepage et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The SSPE method outperforms the existing real-time phase estimation methods in almost all cases.
source: We show that the SSPE method outperforms the existing real-time phase estimation methods in almost all cases.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation and in vivo data results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The state space model separates what is observed (called the observation equation) from what we wish to estimate (called the state equation).
source: This type of model (called a state space model) separates what is observed (called the observation equation) from what we wish to estimate (called the state equation).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the structure of state space models.

claim: The state equation attempts to capture the underlying, unobserved dynamics of the system, while the observation equation transforms the state into the observed signal.
source: The state equation attempts to capture the underlying, unobserved dynamics of the system, while the observation equation transforms the state into the observed signal.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the components of state space models.

claim: An optimal prediction for the state is generated using a Kalman filter that compares the initial prediction of the observation with the actual observed value.
source: We generate an optimal prediction for the state using a Kalman filter that compares the initial prediction of the observation with the actual observed value.
evidence: This is a direct statement about how the Kalman filter is used in the SSPE method.

claim: Each state variable represents an oscillator with a fixed frequency that undergoes small random perturbations.
source: Each state variable represents an oscillator with a fixed frequency that undergoes small random perturbations.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model structure.

claim: The observed data are assumed to be noisy versions of these oscillators.
source: We assume that the observed data are noisy versions of these oscillators.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model assumptions.

claim: The state space model framework combines information from two models: (1) a state model that describes the oscillator dynamics and (2) an observation model that describes how the oscillator generates the data.
source: The state space model framework combines information from two models: (1) a state model that describes the oscillator dynamics and (2) an observation model that describes how the oscillator generates the data.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the structure of the state space model framework.

claim: A linear state equation is implemented that models the real and imaginary part of the complex valued analytic signal of rhythms present in the neural data.
source: We implement a linear state equation that models the real and imaginary part of the complex valued analytic signal of rhythms present in the neural data.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the implementation of the SSPE method.

claim: For each rhythm modeled, the state equation dynamics rotate the analytic signal at that rhythm's frequency.
source: For each rhythm modeled, the state equation dynamics rotate the analytic signal at that rhythm's frequency.
evidence: This is a direct statement about how the state equation operates.

claim: The observation equation sums the real part of the analytic signals of every modeled rhythm to predict the observed neural activity.
source: The observation equation sums the real part of the analytic signals of every modeled rhythm to predict the observed neural activity.
evidence: This is a direct statement about how the observation equation operates.

claim: This state space model structure allows derivation of the amplitude and phase of each modeled rhythm, and estimation of the analytic signal in the temporal domain.
source: This state space model structure allows us to derive the amplitude and phase of each modeled rhythm, and estimate the analytic signal in the temporal domain, thus avoiding complications associated with windowing (i.e., the need to choose large enough window sizes to support sufficient frequency resolution and the associated unavoidable temporal delay in phase estimates) that occur in related frequency domain approaches (Kim et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the advantages of the SSPE method.

claim: The state space model is linear in the state evolution (dynamics of state transitions) and observation equations.
source: The state space model is linear in the state evolution (dynamics of state transitions) and observation equations.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model structure.

claim: The covariance for the state (which determines the bandwidth for the rhythms) and noise for the observation is Gaussian (white noise).
source: Further, the covariance for the state (which determines the bandwidth for the rhythms) and noise for the observation is Gaussian (white noise).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model assumptions.

claim: The assumptions of linearity and Gaussianity imply that the Kalman filter can be used to correct the state estimate based on the true observation.
source: These assumptions (linearity and Gaussianity) imply that we can use the Kalman filter to correct the state estimate based on the true observation (i.e., to filter the state) (Kalman, 1960).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the foundational work on Kalman filtering.

claim: This type of modeling approach has been successfully applied in many contexts to track latent structure from observed data while accounting for state and observation noise effects.
source: This type of modeling approach has been successfully applied in many contexts to track latent structure from observed data while accounting for state and observation noise effects (Brockwell et al., 2004; Eden et al., 2018; Galka et al., 2004; Yousefi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The driving noise for the state U is Gaussian.
source: The driving noise for the state U is Gaussian, a 2N × T matrix with covariance structure Q, a 2N × 2N diagonal matrix with the same variance for the real and imaginary parts of each rhythm.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model assumptions.

claim: Under the EM approach, optimization of parameters follows a two-step process.
source: Under the EM approach, optimization of parameters follows a two-step process. First, initial values for parameters are selected, usually from prior knowledge such as an examination of the power spectrum of an initial data sample. This allows the algorithm to estimate the expectations for the state and the observation. Second, using the state and observation estimates, an analytic solution exists (Shumway and Stoffer, 1982) for the parameters that maximizes the likelihood.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the EM algorithm and is supported by a citation.

claim: The expectation and maximization procedures are repeated until the parameter estimates do not change between two iterations beyond a threshold.
source: We repeat the expectation and maximization procedures until the parameter estimates do not change between two iterations beyond a threshold.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the convergence criterion for the EM algorithm.

claim: The rate of convergence of the EM algorithm depends on the initial parameter estimates and the signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) of the rhythms present in the signal.
source: The rate of convergence of the EM algorithm (speed of computation) depends on the initial parameter estimates and the signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) of the rhythms present in the signal.
evidence: This is a direct statement about factors affecting the EM algorithm's convergence.

claim: In simulations, the first 2 s of data are used to fit the model parameters unless otherwise specified.
source: In simulations, unless otherwise specified, we use the first 2 s of data to fit the model parameters.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the simulation methodology.

claim: With model parameters estimated and fixed, a Kalman filter is applied to predict and update the state estimates, and estimate the phase and amplitude for each oscillator for every sample.
source: With these model parameters estimated and fixed, we then apply a Kalman filter to predict and update the state estimates, and estimate the phase and amplitude for each oscillator, each representing a different rhythm, for every sample (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the method and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The Kalman filter is an optimal filter, achieving minimum error and providing an unbiased estimate of the mean phase in the presence of Gaussian noise.
source: We note that the Kalman filter is an optimal filter, that is, in the presence of Gaussian noise, the Kalman filter achieves minimum error and is an unbiased estimate of the mean phase.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the properties of the Kalman filter.

claim: If the noise is not Gaussian, the Kalman filter remains the optimal linear filter for phase estimation under this model.
source: However, if the noise is not Gaussian, the Kalman filter remains the optimal linear filter for phase estimation under this model.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the robustness of the Kalman filter.

claim: Given the stochastic frequency modulation that is possible under the model, the Kalman filter is robust to small shifts in the central frequency of the rhythm.
source: Given the stochastic frequency modulation that is possible under the model, the Kalman filter is robust to small shifts in the central frequency of the rhythm.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the robustness of the Kalman filter in the context of the SSPE model.

claim: To estimate confidence in the mean phase estimates, 10,000 samples are drawn from the posterior distribution of each state, and from this the width of the 95% credible intervals for the phase is estimated.
source: To do so, we sample 10,000 samples from the posterior distribution of each state j, and from this estimate the width of the 95% credible intervals for the phase.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the method for computing credible intervals.

claim: The credible intervals are derived from the posterior distribution of the state, which is Gaussian; however, following their transformation into angles, the intervals are not constrained to be symmetric.
source: The credible intervals are derived from the posterior distribution of the state, which is Gaussian; however, following their transformation into angles, the intervals are not constrained to be symmetric.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the properties of the credible intervals.

claim: The Zrenner algorithm uses an FIR filter (applied forward and backward) and the Hilbert transform as the core phase estimation technique.
source: The Zrenner algorithm uses an FIR filter (applied forward and backward) and the Hilbert transform as the core phase estimation technique.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the Zrenner method.

claim: The AR model used in the Zrenner algorithm to forecast the data is fitted to the 30th order and efficiently updated on every new sample.
source: The AR model used to forecast the data and allow real-time phase estimation (by expanding the window for the FIR filter) is fitted to the 30th order and efficiently updated on every new sample.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the Zrenner method.

claim: In Blackwood et al., 2018, the authors develop a forward bandpass filter – AR-based (fifth-order AR model whose parameters are fit every second) forecasting and then the Hilbert transform – to compute the phase.
source: In Blackwood et al., 2018, the authors develop a forward bandpass filter – AR-based (fifth-order AR model whose parameters are fit every second) forecasting and then the Hilbert transform – to compute the phase.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the Blackwood method and is supported by a citation.

claim: A Hilbert transformer (of order 18) is applied that estimates the phase by directly computing the Hilbert transform while filtering the data.
source: Here, we instead apply a Hilbert transformer (of order 18) that estimates the phase by directly computing the Hilbert transform while filtering the data as implemented in Blackwood, 2019.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the modified Blackwood method used in this study.

claim: Application of the original and modified Blackwood methods produced consistent phase estimates in sample data.
source: We verified in sample data that application of the original and modified Blackwood methods produced consistent phase estimates.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the validation of the modified method.

claim: Existing studies compare causal, real-time phase estimation approaches to an acausal estimate of phase computed by applying an (acausal) FIR filter and the Hilbert transform.
source: Existing studies compare causal, real-time phase estimation approaches to an acausal estimate of phase computed by applying an (acausal) FIR filter and the Hilbert transform (Blackwood et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2013; Zrenner et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A least-squares linear-phase FIR filter of order 750, with bandpass 4–8 Hz is applied for acausal phase estimation.
source: To maintain consistency with the existing literature, we do so here and apply a least-squares linear-phase FIR filter of order 750, with bandpass 4–8 Hz.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the method used for acausal phase estimation.

claim: After forward and backward filtering of the data, the Hilbert transform is applied to compute the analytic signal.
source: After forward and backward filtering of the data (using MATLAB's filtfilt function), we apply the Hilbert transform to compute the analytic signal (using MATLAB's hilbert function).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the method used for acausal phase estimation.

claim: This acausal estimate of phase has been proposed to serve as a lower bound in phase estimation error for methods that apply a filter-based approach to real-time phase estimation.
source: This acausal estimate of phase has been proposed to serve as a lower bound in phase estimation error for methods that apply a filter-based approach to real-time phase estimation (Zrenner et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The circular standard deviation of the difference between the estimated phase and true phase is used as the error metric.
source: We follow Zrenner et al., 2020, and use the circular standard deviation of the difference between the estimated phase and true phase
evidence: This is a direct statement about the error metric used and is supported by a citation.

claim: The circular standard deviation captures the variance in the circular error for the phase estimate and ignores any potential bias (non-zero mean shift).
source: The circular standard deviation (a transformed version of the phase locking value) captures the variance in the circular error for the phase estimate and ignores any potential bias (non-zero mean shift).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the properties of the error metric.

claim: All rhythms are simulated for 10 s at a sampling rate of 1000 Hz, with a central frequency of 6 Hz.
source: We simulate all rhythms for 10 s at a sampling rate of 1000 Hz, with a central frequency of 6 Hz.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the simulation parameters.

claim: For the first type of rhythm simulated, a pure sinusoid with added white noise is generated.
source: The first type of rhythm we simulate is a pure sinusoid with added white noise
evidence: This is a direct statement about the simulation approach.

claim: For the second type of rhythm simulated, a pure sinusoid with added pink noise is generated.
source: The second type of rhythm we simulate is a pure sinusoid with added pink noise, that is, the power spectral density (PSD) of the noise decreases with the reciprocal of frequency (f)
evidence: This is a direct statement about the simulation approach.

claim: The state in the state space model is an AR model of order 2 (equivalently, a damped harmonic oscillator driven by noise), which has been proposed to capture features of gamma rhythms in visual cortex and rhythms in EEG.
source: The state in the state space model is an AR model of order 2 (West, 1997) (equivalently, a damped harmonic oscillator driven by noise), which has been proposed to capture features of gamma rhythms in visual cortex and rhythms in EEG (Franaszczuk and Blinowska, 1985; Xing et al., 2012; Burns et al., 2010; Spyropoulos et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: For all simulation scenarios, an independent measure of the true phase is available.
source: Thus, in all simulation scenarios, we have an independent measure of the true phase.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the simulation methodology.

claim: Each simulation is repeated 1000 times with different noise instantiations.
source: We repeat each simulation 1000 times with different noise instantiations and calculate error as the circular variance of the difference between the estimated phase and true phase (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the simulation methodology.

claim: For rhythms with narrowband spectral peaks (sine in white noise and sine in pink noise), all estimators perform well, and those estimators that presume a narrowband signal perform best.
source: We find that for rhythms with narrowband spectral peaks (sine in white noise and sine in pink noise, Figure 2B and C), all estimators perform well, and those estimators that presume a narrowband signal (i.e., the filter-based approaches) perform best.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2.

claim: For rhythms with broad spectral peaks (filtered pink noise and state space model), the SSPE method outperforms the other causal approaches.
source: However, for rhythms with broad spectral peaks (filtered pink noise and state space model, Figure 2B and C), the SSPE method outperforms the other causal approaches.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2.

claim: The SSPE method performs as well as (filtered pink noise), or better than (state space model), the acausal FIR method for rhythms with broad spectral peaks.
source: Moreover, the SSPE method performs as well as (filtered pink noise), or better than (state space model), the acausal FIR method.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results.

claim: The SSPE method performs well in all four simulation scenarios and outperforms existing causal phase estimation methods in two instances with broad spectral peaks.
source: We conclude that the SSPE method performs well in all four simulation scenarios and outperforms existing causal phase estimation methods in two instances with broad spectral peaks.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the simulation results.

claim: Multiple alpha rhythms can coexist in EEG.
source: To replicate a situation that has been documented in EEG (e.g., multiple alpha rhythms coexisting) (VanRullen, 2016) and in LFP (e.g., multiple theta/alpha rhythms in hippocampus) (Tort et al., 2010), we simulate two rhythms with similar frequencies.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Multiple theta/alpha rhythms can coexist in hippocampus LFP.
source: To replicate a situation that has been documented in EEG (e.g., multiple alpha rhythms coexisting) (VanRullen, 2016) and in LFP (e.g., multiple theta/alpha rhythms in hippocampus) (Tort et al., 2010), we simulate two rhythms with similar frequencies.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The SSPE method provides an alternative approach to identify two (or potentially more) rhythms without filtering and then allows tracking of the appropriate target rhythm.
source: The SSPE method provides an alternative approach to identify the two (or potentially more) rhythms without filtering and then allows tracking of the appropriate target rhythm.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the capabilities of the SSPE method.

claim: The SSPE method provides estimates of the amplitude and phase of all modeled rhythms.
source: Further, while we focus on the phase of the target rhythm here, we note that the SSPE method provides estimates of the amplitude and phase of all modeled rhythms.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the capabilities of the SSPE method.

claim: Visual inspection suggests that only the SSPE method accurately tracks the target phase when two rhythms are present.
source: Visual inspection for this example (Figure 3B) suggests that only the SSPE method accurately tracks the target phase.
evidence: This claim is based on visual inspection of Figure 3B.

claim: For all methods, the error increases as the frequency of the confounding rhythm approaches the frequency of the target rhythm (6 Hz).
source: For all methods, the error increases as the frequency of the confounding rhythm approaches the frequency of the target rhythm (6 Hz, Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The increased error is restricted to a narrower frequency interval for the SSPE method compared to other methods.
source: However, the increased error is restricted to a narrower frequency interval for the SSPE method.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results.

claim: For the existing causal phase estimators, the error likely reflects choices in the filtering procedure and modeling procedure.
source: For the existing causal phase estimators, the error likely reflects choices in the filtering procedure (i.e., type of filter, features of passband and stopband, window size, see Sameni and Seraj, 2017) and modeling procedure (i.e., AR order, number of samples forecasted; Chen et al., 2013; Zrenner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference about the sources of error in existing methods, supported by citations.

claim: For the acausal FIR estimator, the error likely reflects the filter passband of 4–8 Hz, with increasing error as the confounding rhythm nears the 6 Hz target rhythm.
source: Similarly, for the acausal FIR estimator, the error likely reflects the filter passband of 4–8 Hz, with increasing error as the confounding rhythm nears the 6 Hz target rhythm.
evidence: This is an inference about the sources of error in the acausal FIR method.

claim: For the existing causal and acausal methods, error also increases as the confounding oscillation amplitude increases.
source: For the existing causal and acausal methods, error also increases as the confounding oscillation amplitude increases (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Unlike existing methods, the SSPE method estimates parameters for both the target and confounding rhythms, and tracks each oscillation independently.
source: Unlike these existing methods, the SSPE method estimates parameters for both the target and confounding rhythms, and tracks each oscillation independently.
evidence: This is a direct statement about how the SSPE method differs from existing methods.

claim: By estimating parameters for both rhythms, the SSPE method accounts for the confounding effect of the nearby oscillation and allows more accurate tracking of the target rhythm.
source: By doing so, the SSPE method accounts for the confounding effect of the nearby oscillation and allows more accurate tracking of the target rhythm.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the advantages of the SSPE method.

claim: The SSPE method outperforms existing methods in the case of two simultaneous rhythms with nearby frequencies.
source: We conclude that the SSPE method outperforms these existing methods in the case of two simultaneous rhythms with nearby frequencies.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the simulation results.

claim: Phase resets are defined as consecutive samples of data that show a sudden shift in the oscillatory phase.
source: Phase resets are defined as consecutive samples of data that show a sudden shift in the oscillatory phase, proposed to represent the presence of synchronization of a neural mass in response to a stimulus, for example (Lakatos et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a definition supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Phase resets are common and well documented in electrophysiologic recordings.
source: Phase resets are common and well documented in electrophysiologic recordings (Fiebelkorn et al., 2011; Makeig et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Recent work delivering electrical stimulation based on phase of the theta rhythm has been forced to avoid segments with phase resets to reduce error in real-time phase estimation.
source: Recent work delivering electrical stimulation based on phase of the theta rhythm has been forced to avoid segments with phase resets to reduce error in real-time phase estimation (Gordon et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Accurate tracking of phase resets would provide better evidence for the relevance of phase resetting in generating event related potentials.
source: Further, accurate tracking of phase resets would provide better evidence for the relevance of phase resetting in generating event related potentials (Sauseng et al., 2007) – an analysis that could also be performed acausally.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential utility of accurate phase reset tracking, supported by a citation.

claim: Phase reset is simulated as a shift in the phase of a 6 Hz sinusoid by 90 degrees at four points in a 10 s signal.
source: To do so, we simulate phase reset as a shift in the phase of a 6 Hz sinusoid by 90 degrees at four points in a 10 s signal (example in Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the simulation approach, illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: The error of each phase estimation method is computed in the 167 ms (one period of a 6 Hz rhythm) following the phase reset.
source: We then compute the error of each phase estimation method in the 167 ms (one period of a 6 Hz rhythm) following the phase reset.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the analysis approach.

claim: Visual inspection suggests that only the SSPE method accurately tracks the phase in the interval following the reset.
source: Visual inspection of an example phase reset (Figure 4B) suggests that only the SSPE method accurately tracks the phase in the interval following the reset.
evidence: This claim is based on visual inspection of Figure 4B.

claim: SSPE parameters are fit using an initial 2 s interval containing no phase resets.
source: We note that we fit SSPE parameters using an initial 2 s interval containing no phase resets (Equation 15).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the methodology.

claim: Repeating the analysis for 1000 simulated signals (4000 total phase resets), the error of the SSPE method is significantly lower than the error of the other methods.
source: Repeating this analysis for 1000 simulated signals (4000 total phase resets), we find consistent results; the error of the SSPE method is significantly lower than the error of the other methods (p ~ 0 in all cases using two-sided t-test, see Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of simulation results.

claim: The existing causal and acausal methods implemented are unable to estimate the phase accurately immediately after a phase reset.
source: These results demonstrate that the existing causal and acausal methods implemented here are unable to estimate the phase accurately immediately after a phase reset.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the simulation results.

claim: Each method eventually converged to accurate phase estimation after a phase reset, with the SSPE method converging most rapidly.
source: We find that each method eventually converged to accurate phase estimation after a phase reset, with the SSPE method converging most rapidly (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the convergence time analysis in Table 1.

claim: The differences between methods in convergence time likely result from the windowing used by each method when estimating the phase.
source: The differences between methods likely result from the windowing used by each method when estimating the phase; smaller windows will lead to less impact of the phase reset on the error (as seen with the Blackwood approach converging more quickly than the Zrenner method), with the SSPE needing a window of a single sample.
evidence: This is an inference about the sources of differences in convergence time.

claim: All existing methods require a bandpass filtering step, which limits the fastest rate at which the phase can change (instantaneous frequency).
source: We note that these existing methods all require a bandpass filtering step, which limits the fastest rate at which the phase can change (instantaneous frequency Boashash, 1991).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of existing methods, supported by a citation.

claim: The SSPE method does not require the phase change within a limited range of instantaneous frequencies and therefore can track rapid changes in phase.
source: The SSPE method, however, does not require the phase change within a limited range of instantaneous frequencies and therefore can track rapid changes in phase.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the capabilities of the SSPE method.

claim: The SSPE method is able to most rapidly track the true phase after a phase reset and thus provides the most accurate estimate.
source: We conclude that the SSPE method is able to most rapidly track the true phase after a phase reset and thus provides the most accurate estimate.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the simulation results.

claim: To generate a signal with different SNR, pink noise is filtered into the band of interest, and then additional (unfiltered) pink noise is added.
source: To generate a signal we filter pink noise into the band of interest (see Materials and methods: Signal-to-noise ratio), and then add additional (unfiltered) pink noise.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the simulation approach.

claim: The ratio of the standard deviations of the signal and noise defines the SNR.
source: The ratio of the standard deviations of the signal and noise defines the SNR; we modulate the standard deviation of the signal to achieve the desired SNR.
evidence: This is a direct statement about how SNR is defined and controlled.

claim: The full observation is normalized so that amplitudes across simulations are consistent.
source: Finally, we normalize the full observation so that amplitudes across simulations are consistent.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the simulation approach.

claim: In the SNR simulations, the SNR varies from 1 (signal and noise have the same total power) to 10 (signal has 100 times the total power of the noise).
source: In these simulations the SNR varies from 1 (signal and noise have the same total power) to 10 (signal has 100 times the total power of the noise); see example traces of the observation under each SNR in Figure 5A.i–iv, and see example spectra under each SNR in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the simulation parameters, illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: Each SNR simulation is repeated 1000 times with different noise instantiations.
source: We repeat each simulation 1000 times with different noise instantiations for each SNR.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the simulation methodology.

claim: The credible intervals track with the SNR; signals with higher SNR correspond to smaller credible intervals.
source: As expected, the credible intervals track with the SNR (Figure 5B.i); signals with higher SNR correspond to smaller credible intervals.
evidence: This claim is supported by the results shown in Figure 5B.i.

claim: At low SNR, an arbitrary amplitude threshold would eliminate all data at SNR = 1 and preserve all data at SNR = 2.5.
source: This suggests that, at low SNR, an arbitrary amplitude threshold (e.g., amplitude >1) would eliminate all data at SNR = 1 and preserve all data at SNR = 2.5.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of amplitude distributions.

claim: Using the credible interval width allows identification of transient periods of confidence at both SNR = 1 and SNR = 2.5.
source: Alternatively, using the credible interval width allows identification of transient periods of confidence (e.g., credible interval width <40 degrees) at both SNR values.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of credible interval distributions.

claim: The credible interval width provides a more intuitive threshold than the amplitude, whose intrinsic meaning at any particular value is only understood relatively.
source: We also note that the credible interval width – in units of degrees – provides a more intuitive threshold than the amplitude, whose intrinsic meaning at any particular value is only understood relatively.
evidence: This is a statement about the interpretability of the credible interval width compared to amplitude.

claim: In this simulation study, amplitude serves as a less accurate criterion for confidence in phase compared to the credible interval width.
source: These results suggest that, in this simulation study, amplitude serves as a less accurate criterion for confidence in phase compared to the credible interval width.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the simulation results.

claim: The error for the SSPE method reduces more quickly than for the other methods as SNR increases.
source: We find that the error for the SSPE method reduces more quickly than for the other methods, and at an SNR of 1, the SSPE method is comparable to or better than the contemporary methods of real-time phase estimation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 5C.

claim: At SNR = 10, the error in the SSPE phase estimation is comparable to the acausal FIR.
source: At SNR = 10, the error in the SSPE phase estimation is comparable to the acausal FIR, while the alternative real-time algorithms continue to perform with error similar to an SNR of 1.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 5C.

claim: For the two existing real-time phase estimation methods, broadband rhythms are difficult to track even with high SNR.
source: These results suggest that, for the two existing real-time phase estimation methods, broadband rhythms are difficult to track even with high SNR, consistent with Figure 2C.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the simulation results.

claim: The SSPE method is applied to an example LFP recording from rodent infralimbic cortex, which contains frequent intervals of theta band (4–8 Hz) activity.
source: We first apply the SSPE method to an example LFP recording from rodent infralimbic cortex (see Materials and methods), which contains frequent intervals of theta band (4–8 Hz) activity.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the in vivo data analysis.

claim: In the in vivo signal, the target rhythm changes in time (e.g., time intervals exist with, and without, the theta rhythm).
source: Unlike the simulated data considered above, in the in vivo signal, the target rhythm changes in time (e.g., time intervals exist with, and without, the theta rhythm).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the characteristics of the in vivo data.

claim: Comparing the estimated phase to the true phase, the phase error tends to remain consistent in time.
source: However, comparing the estimated phase to the true phase (see Materials and methods), we find that the phase error tends to remain consistent in time (blue curve in Figure 6A; circular standard deviation 95% interval = [33.11, 75.39]; for error of phase estimates computed using alternative methods, see Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There is no evidence of a linear trend in error with time in the rodent LFP data.
source: We find no evidence of a linear trend in error with time (linear fit, slope = 0.01, p = 0.53); that is, we find no evidence that the error increases in time.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the error over time.

claim: Visual inspection suggests that the error increases when the spectral content of the LFP changes.
source: Instead, visual inspection suggests that the error increases when the spectral content of the LFP changes (e.g., near 120 s in Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is based on visual inspection of Figure 6B.

claim: The error bounds are within the bounds of the range expected for real-time phase estimates in Zrenner et al., 2020.
source: We note that the error bounds are within the bounds of the range expected for real-time phase estimates in Zrenner et al., 2020.
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: Visual inspection of the PSD demonstrates that the theta band power appears more closely matched by a broadband peak, rather than a narrowband peak.
source: Finally, we note that visual inspection of the PSD (Figure 6C) demonstrates that the theta band power appears more closely matched by a broadband peak, rather than a narrowband peak.
evidence: This claim is based on visual inspection of Figure 6C.

claim: There is no evidence that the distribution of phase errors changes for the refit models compared to the original fixed parameter model for the immediate 30 s that followed.
source: We find no evidence that the distribution of phase errors changes for the refit models compared to the original fixed parameter model for the immediate 30 s that followed (p = 0.21, Wilcoxon rank sum test) or for the entire time period analyzed (red interval in Figure 6A, circular standard deviation 95% interval = [30.68, 88.7] degrees; p = 0.35 using Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The original fixed parameter SSPE model (fit using the first 10 s of data) performs as well as the models refit with future data.
source: The original fixed parameter SSPE model (fit using the first 10 s of data; blue curve in Figure 6A) performs as well as the models refit with future data.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Under the assumption that parameters for the frequency band of interest are stable, SSPE model parameters can be estimated whenever there exists a consistent rhythm of interest and then applied to estimate phase at future times.
source: We conclude that, under the assumption that parameters for the frequency band of interest are stable, we are able to estimate the SSPE model parameters whenever there exists a consistent rhythm of interest and then apply this model to estimate phase at future times (here on the scale of hundreds of seconds).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the in vivo data analysis.

claim: For the rodent LFP data, any 10 s interval with sufficiently strong theta rhythm can be used to fit parameters before the model is applied causally.
source: In other words, for these data, any 10 s interval with sufficiently strong theta rhythm can be used to fit parameters before the model is applied causally.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the in vivo data analysis.

claim: The SSPE model parameters can be fit using an initial segment of data, and then applied to derive causal estimates of future phase values.
source: This result has an important practical implication; the SSPE model parameters can be fit using an initial segment of data, and then applied to derive causal estimates of future phase values.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the in vivo data analysis.

claim: The model has robust estimation properties; parameters estimated early in the recording remain appropriate for future observations.
source: In other words, the model has robust estimation properties; parameters estimated early in the recording remain appropriate for future observations.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the in vivo data analysis.

claim: Through direct fitting of the state space model to the time series data, consistent model parameters are found that accurately track the observed theta rhythm.
source: Here, through direct fitting of the state space model to the time series data, we find consistent model parameters that accurately track the observed theta rhythm.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the in vivo data analysis.

claim: The consistency in model parameters is maintained through variations in the rhythm's amplitude.
source: This consistency is maintained through variations in the rhythm's amplitude.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the in vivo data analysis.

claim: The theta rhythm in infralimbic LFP maintains a consistent underlying rhythmic structure over the entire duration of the observation.
source: These observations suggest that the theta rhythm in infralimbic LFP maintains a consistent underlying rhythmic structure over the entire duration of the observation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the in vivo data analysis.

claim: Past approaches to causally estimate phase have not attempted to quantify confidence in the phase estimate beyond utilizing the amplitude as a surrogate.
source: Past approaches to causally estimate phase have not attempted to quantify confidence in the phase estimate beyond utilizing the amplitude as a surrogate (Zrenner et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Using the amplitude assumes a monotonic linear relationship between the phase confidence bounds and the amplitude, which may not be true.
source: However, using the amplitude assumes a monotonic linear relationship between the phase confidence bounds and the amplitude, which may not be true (e.g., for an AR(2) process with complex roots, Spyropoulos et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The SSPE method provides real-time estimates of the credible interval estimates for the phase.
source: Unlike existing methods, the SSPE method provides real-time estimates of the credible interval estimates for the phase (resulting from estimating the parameters of the SSPE model and tracking the phase using the Kalman filter; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the capabilities of the SSPE method.

claim: During a prominent theta rhythm, the credible intervals tightly track the mean phase estimate; at other times – when the theta rhythm is less obvious – the credible intervals expand.
source: We note that, during a prominent theta rhythm, the credible intervals tightly track the mean phase estimate; at other times – when the theta rhythm is less obvious – the credible intervals expand.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of the in vivo LFP data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Error in the phase estimate can be restricted by examining only samples with small CI width.
source: We can restrict error in the phase estimate by examining only samples with small CI width.
evidence: This is a direct statement about a strategy for improving phase estimates.

claim: When thresholding at 10 degrees of credible interval width, the error decreases from (mean) 46.9 (s.e. 0.89) degrees to 26.91 (s.e. 1.07) degrees, while still retaining 27% of the data.
source: When thresholding at 10 degrees of credible interval width, we find that the error decreases from (mean) 46.9 (s.e. 0.89) degrees to 26.91 (s.e. 1.07) degrees, while still retaining 27% of the data.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of the in vivo LFP data.

claim: This error reduction is within the current state-of-the-art in phase estimation with minimum of 20–40 degrees error as a function of SNR.
source: This is within the current state-of-the-art in phase estimation with minimum of 20–40 degrees error as a function of SNR (when applying a sufficiently high amplitude threshold, Zrenner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: Previous studies have proposed a relationship between the theta amplitude envelope and confidence in the phase.
source: Previous studies have proposed a relationship between the theta amplitude envelope, estimated using the traditional approach of narrowband filtering followed by a Hilbert transform, and confidence in the phase (Zrenner et al., 2020); when the theta signal is strong (i.e., the amplitude is large), the theta phase estimate improves.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: When the amplitude is large, small decreases in amplitude coincide with increased credible intervals.
source: Visual inspection reveals that, when the amplitude is large, small decreases in amplitude coincide with increased credible intervals, as expected.
evidence: This claim is based on visual inspection of Figure 7C.i.

claim: Fixed amplitude thresholds produce wide ranges of credible intervals.
source: However, if we choose to approximate certainty in the phase estimate through thresholding the amplitude, we find that fixed amplitude thresholds produce wide ranges of credible intervals (Figure 7C.ii).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7C.ii.

claim: Choosing an amplitude threshold of 65% results in credible intervals that range from 3.8 (2.5th percentile) to 96.8 (97.5th percentile) degrees.
source: This is especially apparent at lower amplitude thresholds; choosing a threshold of 65% results in credible intervals that range from 3.8 (2.5th percentile) to 96.8 (97.5th percentile) degrees.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of the in vivo LFP data.

claim: A fixed amplitude threshold does not guarantee an accurate phase estimate.
source: Therefore, a fixed amplitude threshold does not guarantee an accurate phase estimate.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of the in vivo LFP data.

claim: Inspection of the credible intervals better guides certainty in the phase estimate compared to amplitude thresholds.
source: Instead, we propose that inspection of the credible intervals better guides certainty in the phase estimate.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of the in vivo LFP data.

claim: Credible intervals are directly derived from the modeling procedure, as opposed to surrogate measures of confidence in the phase estimate, such as amplitude.
source: These credible intervals are directly derived from the modeling procedure, as opposed to surrogate measures of confidence in the phase estimate, such as amplitude.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the advantages of credible intervals.

claim: Credible intervals are directly interpretable unlike amplitude thresholds, which depend on the measurement scale.
source: In addition, credible intervals are directly interpretable unlike amplitude thresholds, which depend on the measurement scale (e.g., a credible interval threshold of 10 degrees) versus an amplitude threshold of 10 mV.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the interpretability of credible intervals.

claim: Amplitude is linked to confidence in the phase, however, a fixed amplitude threshold is not directly interpretable and encompasses a wide range of credible interval values.
source: We conclude that amplitude is linked to confidence in the phase, however, a fixed amplitude threshold is not directly interpretable and encompasses a wide range of credible interval values.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of the in vivo LFP data.

claim: The SSPE method is applied to an example EEG recording of the mu rhythm (8–13 Hz) from Zrenner et al., 2020.
source: To illustrate application of the SSPE method in another data modality, we analyze an example EEG recording of the mu rhythm (8–13 Hz) from Zrenner et al., 2020.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the in vivo data analysis.

claim: The SSPE method is applied to track three oscillators (1, 10, 22 Hz) in 10 s intervals in the EEG data.
source: To do so, we apply the SSPE method to track three oscillators (1, 10, 22 Hz) in 10 s intervals (see Materials and methods),and examine the phase estimates of the 8–12 Hz oscillator.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the methodology.

claim: Consistent with the rodent LFP data, refitting of the SSPE model parameters is not required for the EEG data.
source: Consistent with the rodent LFP data, we find that refitting of the SSPE model parameters is not required.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the in vivo EEG data analysis.

claim: The SSPE model parameters estimated from an initial 10 s segment of the EEG produce phase estimation errors consistent with SSPE models refit at future times.
source: Instead, the SSPE model parameters estimated from an initial 10 s segment of the EEG produce phase estimation errors consistent with SSPE models refit at future times (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The mu rhythm in the human EEG data maintains a consistent spectral profile in time and appears to be narrowband.
source: Like the theta rhythm in the LFP rodent data, the mu rhythm in the human EEG data maintains a consistent spectral profile in time (Figure 8B) and further, it appears to be narrowband (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figures 8B and 8C.

claim: Estimating SSPE model parameters early in the EEG data accurately captures the mu rhythm tracked later in the data.
source: Therefore, estimating SSPE model parameters early in the data accurately captures the mu rhythm tracked later in the data, and there is no need to perform the (computationally expensive) refitting of the model.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the in vivo EEG data analysis.

claim: The phase estimates and credible intervals for the mu rhythm reveal how this rhythm waxes and wanes in time.
source: The phase estimates and credible intervals for the mu rhythm reveal how this rhythm waxes and wanes in time (example in Figure 8D and E; for comparison to phase estimates computed using the alternative methods, see Figure 8—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figures 8D and 8E.

claim: When a strong mu rhythm emerges, tight credible intervals surround the mean phase estimate tracking the rhythm of interest; as the mu rhythm wanes, the credible intervals expand.
source: When a strong mu rhythm emerges, tight credible intervals surround the mean phase estimate tracking the rhythm of interest; as the mu rhythm wanes, the credible intervals expand.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of the in vivo EEG data shown in Figure 8.

claim: When restricting analysis to samples with credible interval width less than 25 degrees, the error drops from 40.5 (s.e. 1.1) to 11.2 (s.e. 0.46) degrees while still retaining 16.4% of the data.
source: When we restrict analysis to samples with credible interval width less than 25 degrees, the error drops from 40.5 (s.e. 1.1) to 11.2 (s.e. 0.46) degrees while still retaining 16.4% of the data.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of the in vivo EEG data.

claim: Certainty in phase estimates can be assessed using the credible intervals.
source: As with the LFP, we are able to assess certainty in our phase estimates using the credible intervals.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the in vivo EEG data analysis.

claim: Computing the state estimate including both the 10 and 22 Hz components of the model better approximates the non-sinusoidal waveform of the mu rhythm.
source: Finally, we note that computing the state estimate including both the 10 and 22 Hz components of the model better approximates the non-sinusoidal waveform of the mu rhythm (Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claim: The authors analyze an example EEG recording from Zrenner et al., 2020, in which transcranial magnetic stimulation is used to elicit a motor evoked potential (MEP) from the right abductor pollicis brevis muscle.
source: To illustrate the utility of real-time phase estimation, we again analyze an example EEG recording from Zrenner et al., 2020, in which the authors stimulate a subject at random intervals using transcranial magnetic stimulation to elicit a motor evoked potential (MEP) from the right abductor pollicis brevis muscle.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the in vivo data analysis and is supported by a citation.

claim: The MEP amplitude is analyzed to assess the influence of pre-stimulus mu rhythm phase on the response.
source: We analyze the MEP amplitude to assess the influence of pre-stimulus mu rhythm phase on the response (replicating the analysis performed by Zrenner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the analysis approach and is supported by a citation.

claim: Mu rhythm phase is estimated using the SSPE method with model parameters derived from a different subject.
source: We estimate mu rhythm phase using the SSPE method with model parameters derived from a different subject.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the methodology.

claim: The pre-stimulus phase of the mu rhythm, at the instant immediately prior to stimulation, predicts 13% of the log-transformed MEP amplitude.
source: We find that the pre-stimulus phase of the mu rhythm, at the instant immediately prior to stimulation, predicts (using circular linear regression) 13% of the log-transformed MEP amplitude (Figure 9A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Thresholding the trials using credible interval width improves prediction of the MEP amplitude.
source: Furthermore, thresholding the trials using credible interval width, we find improved prediction of the MEP amplitude.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of the in vivo EEG data.

claim: When using trials with CI width less than 50 degrees, the mu rhythm phase explains 30% of the variance in the MEP amplitude.
source: When using trials with CI width less than 50 degrees, the mu rhythm phase explains 30% of the variance in the MEP amplitude (Figure 9B), and with CI width less than 25 degrees, 48% of the variance (Figure 9C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claim: With CI width less than 25 degrees, the mu rhythm phase explains 48% of the variance in the MEP amplitude.
source: When using trials with CI width less than 50 degrees, the mu rhythm phase explains 30% of the variance in the MEP amplitude (Figure 9B), and with CI width less than 25 degrees, 48% of the variance (Figure 9C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Modulation of the MEP amplitude depends on the pre-stimulus phase of the mu rhythm.
source: These results show that modulation of the MEP amplitude depends on the pre-stimulus phase of the mu rhythm, and suggest that accurate estimation of the mu rhythm (e.g., using the SSPE method with narrow CI width) may enhance the evoked motor response.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of the in vivo EEG data.

claim: Accurate estimation of the mu rhythm using the SSPE method with narrow CI width may enhance the evoked motor response.
source: These results show that modulation of the MEP amplitude depends on the pre-stimulus phase of the mu rhythm, and suggest that accurate estimation of the mu rhythm (e.g., using the SSPE method with narrow CI width) may enhance the evoked motor response.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the analysis of the in vivo EEG data.

claim: To assess the validity of the integration of SSPE into TORTE, a 5 Hz sine wave with no additive noise was generated and the phase was estimated using the MATLAB and C++ implementations.
source: To assess the validity of the integration of SSPE into TORTE (Figure 10A), we generated a 5 Hz sine wave with no additive noise and estimated the phase using the MATLAB and C++ implementations.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the validation approach.

claim: The parameter estimates for the fitted model were computed on the first 10 s of the data.
source: The parameter estimates for the fitted model were computed on the first 10 s of the data.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the methodology.

claim: The computed parameters were nearly identical between the MATLAB and C++ implementations.
source: The computed parameters were nearly identical between the two implementations and the time to estimate the parameters (which, as above, would need to be done only once per experiment) ranged from 2 to 100 s.
evidence: This claim is supported by the validation analysis.

claim: The time to estimate the parameters ranged from 2 to 100 s.
source: The computed parameters were nearly identical between the two implementations and the time to estimate the parameters (which, as above, would need to be done only once per experiment) ranged from 2 to 100 s.
evidence: This claim is supported by the validation analysis.

claim: The phase estimates of the MATLAB and C++ implementations have a mean circular difference of 2.06 degrees with a circular standard deviation of 0.65 degree.
source: The phase estimates of the two implementations have a mean circular difference of 2.06 degrees (Figure 10B) with a circular standard deviation of 0.65 degree; this variation in phase estimates likely arises from differences in filtering in the TORTE real-time (causal filtering on individual buffers) implementation and the offline MATLAB real-time (acausal filtering across all data) implementation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the validation analysis shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The variation in phase estimates likely arises from differences in filtering in the TORTE real-time (causal filtering on individual buffers) implementation and the offline MATLAB real-time (acausal filtering across all data) implementation.
source: The phase estimates of the two implementations have a mean circular difference of 2.06 degrees (Figure 10B) with a circular standard deviation of 0.65 degree; this variation in phase estimates likely arises from differences in filtering in the TORTE real-time (causal filtering on individual buffers) implementation and the offline MATLAB real-time (acausal filtering across all data) implementation.
evidence: This is an inference about the source of variation in phase estimates.

claim: Given that it is a near constant shift in phase, the online learning algorithm in TORTE will correct for the biased phase estimates.
source: Further, given that it is a near constant shift in phase, the online learning algorithm in TORTE will correct for the biased phase estimates.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of the TORTE system.

claim: Across five buffer sizes from 420 to 1700 samples (encompassing 9–37 ms of data), estimating phase with SSPE took less than 0.35 ms in the worst case.
source: Across five buffer sizes from 420 to 1700 samples (encompassing 9–37 ms of data, see Figure 10C), estimating phase with SSPE took less than 0.35 ms in the worst case.
evidence: This claim is supported by the speed analysis shown in Figure 10C.

claim: The system latency of TORTE is in the range of a few milliseconds (driven mainly by the USB-based implementation of the current Open Ephys system), whereas the buffers were evaluated on the scale of microseconds.
source: We note that the system latency of TORTE is in the range of a few milliseconds (driven mainly by the USB-based implementation of the current Open Ephys system), whereas the buffers were evaluated on the scale of microseconds.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the system performance.

claim: The real-time bottleneck lies in signal amplification and digitization, not in the SSPE processing.
source: That is, the real-time bottleneck lies in signal amplification and digitization, not this processing.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the speed analysis.

claim: A real-time implementation of SSPE is presented that could be easily deployed in various experimental setups.
source: In conclusion, we present a real-time implementation of SSPE that could be easily deployed in various experimental setups.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the TORTE implementation.

claim: A new algorithm – the SSPE method – is introduced to track phase in real-time that addresses several limitations of current methods.
source: We introduced a new algorithm – the SSPE method – to track phase in real-time that addresses several limitations of current methods.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the contribution of the manuscript.

claim: In simulation, SSPE performs better than current state-of-the art techniques for real-time phase estimation and comparably, or better, than a commonly used acausal FIR approach.
source: We demonstrated in simulation that SSPE performs better than current state-of-the art techniques for real-time phase estimation and comparably, or better, than a commonly used acausal FIR approach.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the simulation results.

claim: In in vivo data, SSPE model parameters can be estimated and applied for hundreds of seconds without re-estimation.
source: We showed in in vivo data that we can estimate SSPE model parameters and apply them for hundreds of seconds without re-estimation.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the in vivo data results.

claim: Credible intervals from the SSPE method track confidence in the real-time phase estimate, and may provide an intuitive, user-determined decision metric for stimulation at a particular phase.

claim: Future work using the SSPE method in practice may help provide critical evidence on the potential functional importance of phase in neural dynamics.

claim: While brain rhythms tend to be broadband, the most common methods in neuroscience to track a rhythm's phase require appropriate choices of filter parameters and generally expect a narrowband oscillation.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Real-time methods that require a narrowband oscillation struggle to capture the phase accurately for broadband rhythms.

claim: When the broadband rhythm has non-negligible power across all frequencies, the standard non-real-time approach (acausal FIR and Hilbert transform) tracks the phase with limited accuracy.
source: Moreover, when the broadband rhythm has non-negligible power across all frequencies (in which case the phase cycle is more unstable), the standard non-real-time approach (acausal FIR and Hilbert transform) tracks the phase with limited accuracy.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the simulation results.

claim: Implementing the assumption of a broadband peak in the model may improve phase estimation accuracy for forecasting needed in real-time analyses.
source: For forecasting needed in real-time analyses, implementing the same assumption (of a broadband peak) in the model may improve phase estimation accuracy.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential improvements to real-time methods.

claim: In the SSPE method, the assumption of a narrowband oscillation is not required, as the covariance allows flexibility in modeling peaks of different bandwidths.
source: In the SSPE method, the assumption of a narrowband oscillation is not required, as the covariance allows flexibility in modeling peaks of different bandwidths.

source: To address this, the SSPE approach explicitly separates the signal and noise, and models two separate components of noise: state noise and observation noise.

source: The SSPE state consists of harmonic oscillators driven by (white) noise.

claim: The resulting spectrum of the SSPE model consists of broadband peaks at the oscillator frequencies upon a brown aperiodic component, similar to spectra observed in neural field activity.

evidence: This is a direct statement about the capabilities of the SSPE method.
